beats.say: Meera is painting a wall, but not the door and not the two windows. One can covers 10 square metres, and we want to know how many cans to buy.

board.text: Wall 15 m × 8 m, door 2 m × 3 m
2 windows, each 1.5 m × 1.5 m; 1 can covers 10 sq m

beats.say: Start with the whole wall. 15 times 8 is 120 square metres.
Not all of that gets painted. Which parts do we take away from the 120?

ask.ifNot: Read it once more: a door, and two windows, are left unpainted. So all three pieces come off the wall.

beats.say: The door is 2 times 3, which is 6 square metres.
One window is 1.5 times 1.5, which is 2.25. Careful, there are two of them, so that is 4.5 square metres.
Now take them off. 120 minus 6 is 114, and 114 minus 4.5 is 109.5 square metres to paint.
Each can covers 10 square metres, so we divide by 10. 109.5 divided by 10 is 10.95.
But a shop sells whole cans only. So how many must Meera buy?

ask.ifNot: 10 cans would run out just before the wall is finished. She cannot buy part of a can, so she needs one more whole can.

beats.say: We round up, to 11 cans. Look: 10 cans cover only 100 square metres, but 11 cans cover 110, which is enough.
So: the whole area, take away what is left out, divide by what one can covers. And when you are buying, always round up.
Riya's floor is 12 metres by 9 metres, with a square pillar standing in one corner. We want to know how many 30 centimetre tiles cover the rest.

board.text: Floor 12 m × 9 m, pillar 1.5 m × 1.5 m
Square tiles of side 30 cm. How many?

beats.say: First the whole floor. 12 times 9 is 108 square metres.
The pillar is a square, 1.5 by 1.5, which is 2.25 square metres. No tile can go there, so 108 minus 2.25 leaves 105.75.
Now the tile. Its side is in centimetres, but the floor is in metres. What is 30 centimetres, written in metres?

ask.ifNot: 100 centimetres make 1 metre. So 30 centimetres is 30 out of 100 of a metre, and that is 0.3 metres.

beats.say: Mixing metres and centimetres is the big trap here. In metres, one tile is 0.3 times 0.3, which is 0.09 square metres.
How many tiles fit? Divide the floor by one tile. To clear the decimals, multiply both numbers by 100: that is 10575 divided by 9.
10575 divided by 9 is 1175. Riya needs 1175 tiles.
Let's check by multiplying back. 1175 tiles, times 0.09 each, is 105.75 square metres. It fits exactly.
And if we had forgotten the pillar? 108 divided by 0.09 is 1200, which is too many. Always take away what is in the way first.
So: make the units match, take away the part that is not covered, then divide by the area of one tile.
Riya's room is 12 metres by 9 metres, with a square rangoli in the middle. Tiles go everywhere except the rangoli, at 45 rupees for each square metre.

board.text: Room 12 m × 9 m, rangoli 3 m × 3 m
Tiles cost ₹45 per sq m. Total cost = ?

beats.say: First the whole room. 12 times 9 is 108 square metres.
Which area do we pay for?

ask.ifNot: The tiles cover everything except the rangoli. So we want the room with the rangoli taken out.

beats.say: The rangoli is a square, 3 by 3, so it is 9 square metres. And 108 minus 9 leaves 99 square metres to tile.
Each square metre costs 45 rupees, so we need 99 times 45. Here is a neat trick: 99 is just 1 less than 100.
100 times 45 is 4500. Take away one 45, and we get 4455 rupees.
Careful: if we forget to take out the rangoli, we pay for all 108 square metres. That would be 4860 rupees, which is too much.
So: the big shape, minus the piece that is left out, then times the price of one square metre.
Lots of clues here. A rangoli 3 times as long as it is wide, 640 rupees of ribbon round its edge, and powder to fill the inside. We take one clue at a time.

board.text: Powder: ₹2 per sq cm. Cost of powder = ?

beats.say: The ribbon costs 8 rupees for each centimetre, and Arjun spent 640 rupees. So the ribbon is 640 divided by 8, which is 80 centimetres long.
The ribbon runs all the way round the rangoli. So what is that 80 centimetres?

ask.ifNot: A border runs round the outside edge. The distance all the way round a shape is its perimeter.

beats.say: Now picture the sides. Call the breadth 1 part. Then the length is 3 parts. Going all the way round, that is 3 plus 1 plus 3 plus 1, which is 8 parts.
8 parts make 80 centimetres, so one part is 10. The breadth is 10 centimetres, and the length is 3 times that, which is 30.
The powder fills the inside. Which sum tells us how much there is to fill?

ask.ifNot: Powder covers the whole flat inside, and that is area. For a rectangle, area is length times breadth.

beats.say: 30 times 10 is 300. Careful, that is 300 square centimetres, not rupees yet.
Each square centimetre costs 2 rupees. 300 times 2 is 600 rupees.
Check the ribbon clue. Twice 30 plus 10 is 80 centimetres, and 80 times 8 is 640 rupees. It matches.
So the money gave us the perimeter, the perimeter gave us the sides, and the sides gave us the area. One clue at a time.
Raju bends a wire into a triangle with sides 12, 16 and 20 centimetres, and it has a right angle. We want its area.

board.text: Right-angled triangle: sides 12 cm, 16 cm, 20 cm

beats.say: The area of a triangle is half of base times height. And the height must stand straight up from the base, at a right angle.
Two of the sides meet at the right angle. Which two?

ask.ifNot: The longest side, 20, always lies across from the right angle. So the two shorter sides, 12 and 16, are the ones that meet there.

beats.say: So 12 and 16 are our base and height. The 20 is the sloping side, and here is the trap: we do not need it at all.
12 times 16 is 192.
Are we finished?

ask.ifNot: Look back at the rule on the board. It starts with a half, so we still have to halve the 192.

beats.say: Half of 192 is 96. The area is 96 square centimetres.
Why half? Two of these triangles fit together to make a rectangle, 12 by 16. So each triangle is half of that rectangle: 96 and 96 make 192.
So in a right-angled triangle, take the two sides that make the right angle, multiply them, and halve.
Grandma's tablecloth is 120 centimetres by 80 centimetres, with a border 10 centimetres wide all round the inside edge. We want the area of the border only.

board.text: Cloth 120 cm × 80 cm, border 10 cm wide inside the edge

beats.say: The border is like a picture frame. The easy way to find a frame is the whole cloth, minus the middle piece.
The whole cloth is 120 times 80, which is 9600 square centimetres.
Now the middle piece. The border is 10 centimetres wide at each end. So how long is the middle?

ask.ifNot: There is border at the left end and at the right end. So the length loses 10, and then another 10. That leaves 100.

beats.say: That is the trap: the 10 comes off both ends. For the length, 120 minus 10 minus 10 is 100. For the width, 80 minus 10 minus 10 is 60.
So the middle piece is 100 times 60, which is 6000 square centimetres.
The border is what is left. 9600 minus 6000 is 3600 square centimetres.
Let's check it another way, strip by strip. Two long strips, 120 by 10, make 2400. Two short strips, 60 by 10, make 1200. Together that is 3600 again.
So for a border, find the whole, find the middle, and subtract. And remember the width comes off at both ends.
Arjun's ground is 120 metres by 80 metres, with a track 5 metres wide all round the outside. Grass on the track costs 12 rupees for each square metre.

board.text: Ground 120 m × 80 m, track 5 m wide round the outside
Grass on the track: ₹12 per sq m. Cost = ?

beats.say: The track is a frame round the ground. So its area is the big outer rectangle, minus the ground.
The track adds 5 metres at each end of the ground. So how long is the outer rectangle?

ask.ifNot: There is track at both ends of the ground. So the length grows by 5, and then by 5 again. That makes 130.

beats.say: The outer length is 120 plus 5 plus 5, which is 130. The outer breadth is 80 plus 5 plus 5, which is 90.
So the outer rectangle is 130 times 90, which is 11700. And the ground itself is 120 times 80, which is 9600.
Take the ground away. 11700 minus 9600 is 2100 square metres of track.
Now the cost, 2100 times 12. 2100 times 10 is 21000, and 2100 times 2 is 4200.
21000 plus 4200 is 25200. The grass costs 25200 rupees.
The classic slip is adding the 5 only once. A track all the way round adds its width twice to the length, and twice to the breadth.
So for a path round the outside: make the outer rectangle, subtract the inner one, then multiply by the price.
Meera's tablecloth is 90 centimetres by 60 centimetres. She cuts a piece, 30 centimetres by 20 centimetres, out of one corner. How much cloth is left?

board.text: Piece cut from a corner: 30 cm × 20 cm

beats.say: How do we find the area that is left?

ask.ifNot: Cutting a piece out makes the cloth smaller. So we take the area of the piece away from the area of the whole cloth.

beats.say: First the whole cloth, 90 times 60. 9 times 6 is 54, and the two zeros go on the end: 5400 square centimetres.
Now the piece. 30 times 20 is 600 square centimetres.
Take it away. 5400 minus 600 is 4800 square centimetres.
Careful not to subtract the sides first. That would give 60 by 40, which is only 2400. It slices off a whole strip, not just one corner.
Check by putting the piece back. 4800 plus 600 is 5400, the whole cloth.
So when a piece is cut out, work out both areas first, and then subtract the areas, never the sides.
Arjun has a square sheet of side 20 centimetres. He cuts a 4 centimetre square from each corner and folds up the sides to make a tray. We want the area of the flat base.

board.text: A 4 cm square is cut from each corner

beats.say: When the flaps fold up, the flat middle is the base. So first we need to know how long the base is.

board.text: Base = the middle that stays flat

beats.say: Look along one edge of the sheet. There is a corner cut at both ends. How long is the base along that edge?

ask.ifNot: One corner takes 4 off the left end, and another takes 4 off the right end. 20 minus 4, and minus 4 again, leaves 12.

beats.say: That is the trap. Take off 4 only once and you get 16. But there is a corner at each end, so it is 20 minus 4 minus 4, which is 12.
The sheet was a square, so the very same thing happens the other way. The base is a square, 12 by 12.
12 times 12 is 144. The base is 144 square centimetres.
Let's check that every bit of the sheet is counted. The whole sheet is 20 times 20, 400. The four corners are 4 times 16, which is 64.
Each flap is 12 by 4, which is 48, and four of them make 192. Then 144 plus 64 plus 192 is 400, the whole sheet.
So when corners are cut from a sheet, each side of the base loses the cut twice. Then the base is just length times breadth.
Here is an equilateral triangle, and each side is 5.3 centimetres. We want the perimeter, the distance all the way round.

board.text: Equilateral triangle, each side 5.3 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: How many equal sides does it have?

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all the sides are equal, and a triangle has 3 sides.

beats.say: So going round, we walk 5.3 centimetres, 3 times over. A quicker way to write that is 3 times 5.3.
To multiply, split 5.3 into 5 and 0.3. 3 times 5 is 15, and 3 times 0.3 is 0.9.
Put the two pieces together. 15 plus 0.9 is 15.9, so the perimeter is 15.9 centimetres.
Careful not to lose the decimal part. 3 times 5 alone gives 15, but those 3 lots of 0.3 count too.
Check by sharing it back out. 15.9 divided by 3 is 5.3, the side we started with.
So for any shape with equal sides, the perimeter is the number of sides times one side.
A square has a perimeter of 16 centimetres. We want the length of one side.
The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 16?

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 sides, and all 4 are the same length.

beats.say: So 4 equal sides, put end to end, make 16 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 4 equal sides together make 16. To get back to one side, we share 16 equally among 4, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: 16 divided by 4. Well, 4 times 4 is 16, so each side is 4 centimetres.
Careful not to just halve it. Half of 16 is 8, but a square has 4 sides, not 2.
Let's check by going back round. 4 times 4 is 16, the perimeter. It works.
So when all the sides are equal, one side is the perimeter divided by the number of sides.
A rectangle with a perimeter of 40 centimetres and a length of 12 centimetres. We need its breadth.

board.text: Rectangle: perimeter 40 cm, length 12 cm. Breadth = ?

beats.say: Walk round a rectangle and you pass a length, a breadth, another length and another breadth. So the perimeter is 2 lengths and 2 breadths.
So what does half of the perimeter give us?

ask.ifNot: Half of the walk round takes you along one length and one breadth. So half the perimeter is length plus breadth.

beats.say: Half of 40 is 20. So the length and the breadth together make 20.
The length is 12. So the breadth is 20 minus 12, which is 8 centimetres.
Here is the trap. Take both lengths off the 40 and you get 16. But that is two breadths, so it still has to be halved.
Check: 12 plus 8 is 20, and twice 20 is 40. It matches the perimeter.
So to find a missing side of a rectangle, halve the perimeter, then take away the side you know.
A regular hexagon has a perimeter of 54 centimetres. We want the length of one side.

board.text: Regular hexagon, perimeter 54 cm. Each side = ?

beats.say: The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 54?

ask.ifNot: Hex means 6. A hexagon has 6 sides, and regular means they are all the same length.

beats.say: So 6 equal sides, put end to end, make 54 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 6 equal sides together make 54. To get back to one side, we share 54 equally among 6, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: 54 divided by 6. Well, 6 times 9 is 54, so each side is 9 centimetres.
A trap here is to answer 6, the number of sides. The 6 is what we divide by. The side is what comes out, 9.
Let's check by going back round. 6 times 9 is 54, the perimeter. It works.
So when all the sides are equal, one side is the perimeter divided by the number of sides.
This rectangle is twice as long as it is wide, and its perimeter is 42 centimetres. We want both the length and the breadth.
Call the breadth 1 part. Then the length is 2 parts, because it is 2 times as long.
Going all the way round the rectangle, how many parts do we pass?

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth make 3 parts. But the walk round passes two lengths and two breadths, so it is 3 parts, twice over.

beats.say: 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1 is 6 parts. And those 6 parts together are the whole perimeter, 42 centimetres.
So one part is 42 divided by 6, which is 7. That is the breadth: 7 centimetres.
The length is 2 parts. 2 times 7 is 14 centimetres.
The trap is to share 42 among 3 parts only. That forgets we pass every side twice on the way round.
Check: 14 plus 7 is 21, and twice 21 is 42. That is the perimeter, so it all fits.
The plan to keep: turn the sides into parts, count the parts round the whole edge, and divide the perimeter by that.
A square with a perimeter of 20 centimetres. We want its area.
Area needs the side, and all we have is the perimeter. So this takes two steps: first the side, then the area.
A square has 4 equal sides. How do we get one side from the perimeter?

ask.ifNot: The 4 equal sides add up to the perimeter. So one side is the perimeter shared among 4.

beats.say: 20 divided by 4 is 5. Each side is 5 centimetres.
Now for the area of the square. Which sum is it?

ask.ifNot: Area counts the little squares inside: 5 rows, with 5 in each row. That is side times side. 4 times the side only takes us back to the perimeter.

beats.say: 5 times 5 is 25. The area is 25 square centimetres.
Don't stop at 5, that is only the side. And notice that the perimeter, 20, and the area, 25, are different numbers, measuring different things.
Check the first step: 4 sides of 5 make 20, the perimeter we were given.
So from perimeter to area in a square: divide by 4 for the side, then multiply the side by itself.
A rectangle with a perimeter of 50 centimetres, and its length is 5 centimetres more than its breadth. We want the area, so first we need both sides.

board.text: Rectangle: perimeter 50 cm, length = breadth + 5 cm

beats.say: Half of the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Half of 50 is 25.
The length is a breadth with 5 extra. If we take that extra 5 away from the 25, what is left?

ask.ifNot: Without its extra 5, the length is exactly as long as the breadth. So what is left is one breadth, and another breadth.

beats.say: 25 minus 5 is 20, and that is two breadths.
So one breadth is half of 20, which is 10. And the length is 10 plus 5, which is 15.
Now the area, which is length times breadth. 15 times 10 is 150 square centimetres.
Two traps to dodge. Don't stop at the sides, because the question asks for the area. And don't halve the 25 straight away: the extra 5 has to come off first.
Check: 15 plus 10 is 25, and twice 25 is 50. And 15 is 5 more than 10. Both clues fit.
So: halve the perimeter, take off the extra, and halve again for the shorter side. Then it is length times breadth.
A square with an area of 441 square centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter needs the side. And the area of a square is side times side. So we want a number that, multiplied by itself, makes 441.
Let's get close first. 20 times 20 is 400. So what can we say about the side?

ask.ifNot: 400 is smaller than 441. So the side has to be a bit bigger than 20.

beats.say: 441 ends in 1, and 1 times 1 is 1. So let's try 21. 21 times 21 is 441, so the side is 21 centimetres.
Now the perimeter. A square has 4 equal sides, so which sum do we want?

ask.ifNot: The perimeter is the walk round all 4 sides. Each side is 21, so it is 4 times 21.

beats.say: 4 times 21 is 84. The perimeter is 84 centimetres.
Two things to watch. 21 is only the side, so don't stop there. And a perimeter is a length, so it is 84 centimetres, not square centimetres.
Check by going backwards. 84 divided by 4 is 21, and 21 times 21 is 441, the area we were given.
Two steps to keep: the area tells you the side, and 4 times the side is the perimeter.
A rectangle with an area of 98 square centimetres, and its length is double its breadth. We want the perimeter, so we need the sides.

board.text: Rectangle: area 98 sq cm, length = 2 × breadth

beats.say: Here is a picture that helps. If the length is double the breadth, the rectangle is really two equal squares, side by side.
The two squares together have an area of 98. So what is the area of one square?

ask.ifNot: Two equal squares share the 98 between them. So each one is half of 98.

beats.say: Half of 98 is 49. So each square has an area of 49.
Which number, multiplied by itself, makes 49? 7 times 7. So the breadth is 7 centimetres, and the length is double that, 14.
Now the perimeter, 2 lengths and 2 breadths. 14 plus 7 is 21, and twice 21 is 42 centimetres.
Don't stop at 7, or 14, or 21. Those are steps on the way. The question asks for the whole walk round, and that is 42.
Check the area clue: 14 times 7 is 98. It fits.
So when you are given an area, find the sides first. Once you have the sides, the perimeter is easy.
The distance all the way round an equilateral triangle is 23.1 centimetres. How long is each side?

board.text: Equilateral triangle, perimeter 23.1 cm. Each side = ?

beats.say: The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 23.1?

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all the sides are equal, and a triangle has 3 sides.

beats.say: So 3 equal sides, put end to end, make 23.1 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 3 equal sides together make 23.1. To get back to one side, we share 23.1 equally among 3, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: To divide 23.1 by 3, split it into 21 and 2.1. 21 divided by 3 is 7, and 2.1 divided by 3 is 0.7.
7 plus 0.7 is 7.7. Each side is 7.7 centimetres.
Don't drop the decimal part. A side of just 7 would give a perimeter of only 21, and ours is 23.1.
Check: 3 sides of 7.7 make 23.1. That is the perimeter we were given.
The rule to keep: count the equal sides, then divide the perimeter by that number.
An isosceles triangle with a perimeter of 26 centimetres. Each of its two equal sides is 8 centimetres, and we want the third side.

board.text: Equal sides 8 cm each. Third side = ?

beats.say: Isosceles means two sides are equal, and congruent is just another word for equal. So the sides are 8, 8, and one we do not know yet.
What should we work out first?

ask.ifNot: There are two equal sides, and both are part of the perimeter. So first find how much the two of them make together.

beats.say: 8 plus 8 is 16. That is how much of the perimeter the two equal sides use up.
The rest belongs to the third side. 26 minus 16 is 10 centimetres.
The trap is taking away only one 8. That gives 18, but there are two equal sides to take off, not one.
Check by adding all three sides. 8 plus 8 plus 10 is 26. It matches the perimeter.
The plan to keep: perimeter, minus all the sides you already know, leaves the side you want.
Here is a square, and each side is 4.6 centimetres. We want the perimeter, the distance all the way round.
How many equal sides does it have?

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 sides, and all 4 are the same length.

beats.say: So going round, we walk 4.6 centimetres, 4 times over. A quicker way to write that is 4 times 4.6.
To multiply, split 4.6 into 4 and 0.6. 4 times 4 is 16, and 4 times 0.6 is 2.4.
Put the two pieces together. 16 plus 2.4 is 18.4, so the perimeter is 18.4 centimetres.
Now look at the units. A perimeter is a length, so it stays in centimetres. Square centimetres are for area, and nothing here was changed to millimetres.
Check by sharing it back out. 18.4 divided by 4 is 4.6, the side we started with.
So for any shape with equal sides, the perimeter is the number of sides times one side.
This is an equilateral triangle with every side 5.4 centimetres long. The perimeter is how far it is all the way round.

board.text: Equilateral triangle, each side 5.4 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: How many equal sides does it have?

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all the sides are equal, and a triangle has 3 sides.

beats.say: So going round, we walk 5.4 centimetres, 3 times over. A quicker way to write that is 3 times 5.4.
To multiply, split 5.4 into 5 and 0.4. 3 times 5 is 15, and 3 times 0.4 is 1.2.
Put the two pieces together. 15 plus 1.2 is 16.2, so the perimeter is 16.2 centimetres.
Two things to watch. A triangle has 3 sides, not 4. And a perimeter is a length, so it is in centimetres, not square centimetres.
Let's check. Share 16.2 equally among the 3 sides, and each one gets 5.4. That is our side.
So for any shape with equal sides, the perimeter is the number of sides times one side.
A square has a perimeter of 24.4 centimetres. We want the length of one side.
The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 24.4?

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 sides, and all 4 are the same length.

beats.say: So 4 equal sides, put end to end, make 24.4 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 4 equal sides together make 24.4. To get back to one side, we share 24.4 equally among 4, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: To divide 24.4 by 4, split it into 24 and 0.4. 24 divided by 4 is 6, and 0.4 divided by 4 is 0.1.
6 plus 0.1 is 6.1. Each side is 6.1 centimetres.
Now the units. The perimeter was in centimetres, so the side is in centimetres too. Not millimetres, and not square units, which are for area.
Let's check by going back round. 4 times 6.1 is 24.4, the perimeter. It works.
So when all the sides are equal, one side is the perimeter divided by the number of sides.
A rectangle with a perimeter of 48 centimetres and a length of 14 centimetres. We need its breadth.

board.text: Rectangle: perimeter 48 cm, length 14 cm. Breadth = ?

beats.say: Walk round a rectangle and you pass a length, a breadth, another length and another breadth. So the perimeter is 2 lengths and 2 breadths.
So what does half of the perimeter give us?

ask.ifNot: Half of the walk round takes you along one length and one breadth. So half the perimeter is length plus breadth.

beats.say: Half of 48 is 24. So the length and the breadth together make 24.
The length is 14. So the breadth is 24 minus 14, which is 10 centimetres.
Here is the trap. Take both lengths off the 48 and you get 20. But that is two breadths, so it still has to be halved. And keep the unit: centimetres, like the question.
Check: 14 plus 10 is 24, and twice 24 is 48. It matches the perimeter.
So to find a missing side of a rectangle, halve the perimeter, then take away the side you know.
A regular hexagon has a perimeter of 72 centimetres. We want the length of one side.

board.text: Regular hexagon, perimeter 72 cm. Each side = ?

beats.say: The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 72?

ask.ifNot: Hex means 6. A hexagon has 6 sides, and regular means they are all the same length.

beats.say: So 6 equal sides, put end to end, make 72 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 6 equal sides together make 72. To get back to one side, we share 72 equally among 6, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: 72 divided by 6. Well, 6 times 12 is 72, so each side is 12 centimetres.
Careful with the 6 times table. 6 times 10 is 60, and 2 more sixes take us up to 72. So each side is 12.
Check: 6 sides of 12 make 72. That is the perimeter we were given.
So when all the sides are equal, one side is the perimeter divided by the number of sides.
A square with a perimeter of 36 centimetres. We want its area.
Area needs the side, and all we have is the perimeter. So this takes two steps: first the side, then the area.
A square has 4 equal sides. How do we get one side from the perimeter?

ask.ifNot: The 4 equal sides add up to the perimeter. So one side is the perimeter shared among 4.

beats.say: 36 divided by 4 is 9. Each side is 9 centimetres.
Now for the area of the square. Which sum is it?

ask.ifNot: Area counts the little squares inside: 9 rows, with 9 in each row. That is side times side. 4 times the side only takes us back to the perimeter.

beats.say: 9 times 9 is 81. The area is 81 square centimetres.
Careful not to do something quick with the 36, like doubling it. The area always comes from the side, and 9 times 9 is exactly 81.
Check the first step: 4 sides of 9 make 36, the perimeter we were given.
So from perimeter to area in a square: divide by 4 for the side, then multiply the side by itself.
A rectangle with a perimeter of 40 centimetres, and its length is 8 centimetres more than its breadth. We want the area, so first we need both sides.

board.text: Rectangle: perimeter 40 cm, length = breadth + 8 cm

beats.say: Half of the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Half of 40 is 20.
The length is a breadth with 8 extra. If we take that extra 8 away from the 20, what is left?

ask.ifNot: Without its extra 8, the length is exactly as long as the breadth. So what is left is one breadth, and another breadth.

beats.say: 20 minus 8 is 12, and that is two breadths.
So one breadth is half of 12, which is 6. And the length is 6 plus 8, which is 14.
Now the area, which is length times breadth. 14 times 6 is 84 square centimetres.
Careful not to multiply the numbers in the question. 40 is a perimeter and 8 is a difference, so 40 times 8 means nothing here. We need the two sides first.
Check: 14 plus 6 is 20, and twice 20 is 40. And 14 is 8 more than 6. Both clues fit.
So: halve the perimeter, take off the extra, and halve again for the shorter side. Then it is length times breadth.
A square with an area of 676 square centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter needs the side. And the area of a square is side times side. So we want a number that, multiplied by itself, makes 676.
Let's get close first. 25 times 25 is 625. So what can we say about the side?

ask.ifNot: 625 is smaller than 676. So the side has to be a bit bigger than 25.

beats.say: 676 ends in 6, and 6 times 6 ends in 6. So let's try 26. 26 times 26 is 676, so the side is 26 centimetres.
Now the perimeter. A square has 4 equal sides, so which sum do we want?

ask.ifNot: The perimeter is the walk round all 4 sides. Each side is 26, so it is 4 times 26.

beats.say: 4 times 26 is 104. The perimeter is 104 centimetres.
Mind the units. Area is in square centimetres, but a perimeter is a length. So the answer is 104 centimetres, plain centimetres.
Check by going backwards. 104 divided by 4 is 26, and 26 times 26 is 676, the area we were given.
Two steps to keep: the area tells you the side, and 4 times the side is the perimeter.
The length of this rectangle is twice its breadth, and the perimeter is 78 centimetres. We need the length and the breadth.
Call the breadth 1 part. Then the length is 2 parts, because it is 2 times as long.
Going all the way round the rectangle, how many parts do we pass?

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth make 3 parts. But the walk round passes two lengths and two breadths, so it is 3 parts, twice over.

beats.say: 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1 is 6 parts. And those 6 parts together are the whole perimeter, 78 centimetres.
So one part is 78 divided by 6, which is 13. That is the breadth: 13 centimetres.
The length is 2 parts. 2 times 13 is 26 centimetres.
The trap is to share 78 among 3 parts only. That makes both sides twice too big, because we pass every side twice on the way round.
Check: 26 plus 13 is 39, and twice 39 is 78. That is the perimeter, so it all fits.
So when one side is so many times the other, count the parts all the way round, find one part, and build the sides from it.
An equilateral triangle has a perimeter of 29.1 centimetres. We want the length of one side.

board.text: Equilateral triangle, perimeter 29.1 cm. Each side = ?

beats.say: The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 29.1?

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all the sides are equal, and a triangle has 3 sides.

beats.say: So 3 equal sides, put end to end, make 29.1 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 3 equal sides together make 29.1. To get back to one side, we share 29.1 equally among 3, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: To divide 29.1 by 3, split it into 27 and 2.1. 27 divided by 3 is 9, and 2.1 divided by 3 is 0.7.
9 plus 0.7 is 9.7. Each side is 9.7 centimetres.
Careful with the whole part. 3 times 9 is 27, so the side starts with 9, not with 8 or 7.
Let's check by going back round. 3 times 9.7 is 29.1, the perimeter. It works.
The rule to keep: count the equal sides, then divide the perimeter by that number.
A regular hexagon has a perimeter of 42 centimetres. We want the total of just 5 of its sides.

board.text: Regular hexagon, perimeter 42 cm. Sum of 5 sides = ?

beats.say: First, how many equal sides does a regular hexagon have?

ask.ifNot: Hex means 6. A hexagon has 6 sides, and regular means they are all the same length.

beats.say: So 6 equal sides make 42. One side is 42 divided by 6, which is 7 centimetres.
We want 5 of the sides, not all 6. What is the quickest way to get that?

ask.ifNot: 5 sides is all 6 sides with one side left out. So we can take one side, 7, away from the whole perimeter.

beats.say: 42 minus 7 is 35. The 5 sides add up to 35 centimetres.
We can also multiply. 5 sides of 7 centimetres is 35. Two ways, one answer.
The trap is dividing 42 by 5. The 42 belongs to all 6 sides, so we must find one side first.
So with a regular shape, always find one side first. After that you can build any number of sides you like.
Here is a regular hexagon, and each side is 6.1 centimetres. We want the perimeter, the distance all the way round.

board.text: Regular hexagon, each side 6.1 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: How many equal sides does it have?

ask.ifNot: Hex means 6. A hexagon has 6 sides, and regular means they are all the same length.

beats.say: So going round, we walk 6.1 centimetres, 6 times over. A quicker way to write that is 6 times 6.1.
To multiply, split 6.1 into 6 and 0.1. 6 times 6 is 36, and 6 times 0.1 is 0.6.
Put the two pieces together. 36 plus 0.6 is 36.6, so the perimeter is 36.6 centimetres.
Don't drop the little 0.1. It is on all 6 sides, so together it adds 0.6. The answer is 36.6, not just 36.
Check by sharing it back out. 36.6 divided by 6 is 6.1, the side we started with.
The rule to keep: when every side is equal, count the sides and multiply by the length of one.
A triangle with sides 3.2, 4.6 and 5.3 centimetres. The perimeter is the walk all the way round, so we add the three sides.

board.text: Triangle: sides 3.2 cm, 4.6 cm, 5.3 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Add the whole numbers first. 3 plus 4 plus 5 is 12.
Now the tenths: 2 tenths, 6 tenths and 3 tenths. How many tenths is that altogether?

ask.ifNot: Add them like ordinary numbers. 2 plus 6 is 8, and 3 more makes 11. So there are 11 tenths.

beats.say: 11 tenths is more than one whole. It is 1 whole and 1 tenth, which we write as 1.1. This is the step that often gets dropped.
12 plus 1.1 is 13.1. The perimeter is 13.1 centimetres.
Check by adding in order. 3.2 plus 4.6 is 7.8, and 7.8 plus 5.3 is 13.1 again.
So with decimals, add the wholes, add the tenths, and when the tenths go past 10, carry a whole across.
Thrice means 3 times. So this rectangle is 3 times as long as it is wide, and its perimeter is 64 centimetres. We want the breadth.
Call the breadth 1 part. Then the length is 3 parts, because it is 3 times as long.
Going all the way round the rectangle, how many parts do we pass?

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth make 4 parts. But the walk round passes two lengths and two breadths, so it is 4 parts, twice over.

beats.say: 3 plus 1 plus 3 plus 1 is 8 parts. And those 8 parts together are the whole perimeter, 64 centimetres.
So one part is 64 divided by 8, which is 8. And one part is the breadth: 8 centimetres.
The length is 3 parts, so 3 times 8 is 24 centimetres. We were not asked for it, but it helps us check.
Two traps here. Sharing 64 among 4 parts forgets we pass every side twice. And the question wants the breadth, not the length.
Check: 24 plus 8 is 32, and twice 32 is 64. That is the perimeter, so it all fits.
The plan to keep: turn the sides into parts, count the parts round the whole edge, and divide the perimeter by that.
An isosceles triangle with a perimeter of 32 centimetres. Each of its two equal sides is 9 centimetres, and we want the third side.

board.text: Equal sides 9 cm each. Third side = ?

beats.say: Isosceles means two sides are equal, and congruent is just another word for equal. So the sides are 9, 9, and one we do not know yet.
What should we work out first?

ask.ifNot: There are two equal sides, and both are part of the perimeter. So first find how much the two of them make together.

beats.say: 9 plus 9 is 18. That is how much of the perimeter the two equal sides use up.
The rest belongs to the third side. 32 minus 18 is 14 centimetres.
Don't stop at 18. That is the two equal sides together, not the third side. The third side is what is left of the perimeter.
Check by adding all three sides. 9 plus 9 plus 14 is 32. It matches the perimeter.
The plan to keep: perimeter, minus all the sides you already know, leaves the side you want.
A rectangle with a length of 1.2 metres and a breadth of 50 centimetres. We want its area.

board.text: Rectangle: length 1.2 m, breadth 50 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Before we multiply anything, look at the units. What do you notice?

choices: one is metres, one is centimetres
ask.ifNot: Read the two measurements again. The length is in metres, but the breadth is in centimetres. They do not match yet.

beats.say: The answer is wanted in square centimetres, so let's turn the length into centimetres. 1 metre is 100 centimetres.
So 1.2 metres is 1.2 times 100, which is 120 centimetres.
Now both sides are in centimetres, and area is length times breadth. 12 times 5 is 60, and the two zeros go on the end: 6000 square centimetres.
Here is the trap. Multiply 1.2 by 50 straight away and you get 60. But that mixes metres with centimetres, so it means nothing.
So before any area sum, make the units match. Then it is just length times breadth.
A square whose area and perimeter are the very same number. We have to find its side.
Write the two rules side by side. Area is side times side. Perimeter is 4 times the side.
Let's try a small square and watch. With side 2, the area is 2 times 2, which is 4. The perimeter is 4 times 2, which is 8. Not equal.
Look at the two rules again. Both multiply the side by something. When will they give the same answer?

ask.ifNot: One rule multiplies the side by the side, the other multiplies it by 4. They agree when those two are the same, so the side must be 4.

beats.say: Try 4. The area is 4 times 4, which is 16. The perimeter is 4 times 4, which is 16. Equal!
What about 0? The numbers do match, but a square with side 0 is no square at all. So we leave that one out.
And bigger squares? With side 5, the area is 25 but the perimeter is only 20. From here on the area runs ahead, so 4 is the only answer.
So when a question gives a rule but no numbers, write the formulas side by side and test small numbers.
A rectangle with a perimeter of 50 centimetres. Its length is 3 over 2 times its breadth, and we want the area.
3 over 2 times sounds hard, so let's make it easy. Cut the breadth into 2 equal parts. Then the length is 3 of those same parts.
Half of the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Half of 50 is 25.
One length and one breadth together: how many parts is that?

ask.ifNot: The length is 3 parts and the breadth is 2 parts. Together that is 3 plus 2.

beats.say: 3 plus 2 is 5 parts, and they make 25. So one part is 25 divided by 5, which is 5 centimetres.
The breadth is 2 parts: 2 times 5 is 10. The length is 3 parts: 3 times 5 is 15.
Area is length times breadth. 15 times 10 is 150 square centimetres.
Check both clues. Twice 15 plus 10 is 50, the perimeter. And 15 is one and a half times 10. Everything fits.
So when one side is a fraction of the other, turn the sides into equal parts. Find one part, and the rest follows.
Two playgrounds. One is a rectangle, 25 metres by 20 metres. The other is a square with sides of 22 metres. Which one is bigger?
A bigger playground means more room to play. Which measurement tells us that?

ask.ifNot: Room to run about is the flat space inside the edges. That is the area.

beats.say: The rectangle first. 25 times 20 is 500 square metres.
Now the square, 22 times 22. Take it in two bites: 22 times 20 is 440, and 22 times 2 is 44.
440 plus 44 is 484 square metres.
500 is more than 484. So the rectangular playground is the bigger one.
Don't judge by the side lengths. 22 looks big next to 20, but the rectangle has that long 25. Only working out both areas settles it.
So to compare two shapes for size, find the area of each one, then compare the two numbers.
A plot of land is 16 metres long and 10 metres wide. Each square metre costs 1000 rupees. What does the whole plot cost?

board.text: Plot 16 m × 10 m. 1 sq m costs Rs. 1000. Cost = ?

beats.say: The price is for each square metre. So what must we find first?

ask.ifNot: Square metres measure the flat surface of the plot, and that is its area.

beats.say: Area is length times breadth. 16 times 10 is 160 square metres.
Picture 160 squares, each one metre by one metre, and every one of them costs 1000 rupees. So the cost is 160 times 1000.
To multiply by 1000, write 160 and put three zeros after it. That makes 1,60,000 rupees.
Careful with the trap. 16 times 1000 is only 16000. That leaves out the breadth altogether.
Check by dividing back. 1,60,000 divided by 1000 is 160, the area we found.
So for a cost on land or floors, find the area first, then multiply by the price of one square metre.
A ground 30 metres long and 20 metres wide has to be levelled. The charge is 5 rupees for every square metre.

board.text: Ground 30 m × 20 m. Levelling: Rs. 5 per sq m. Cost = ?

beats.say: We pay for every square metre of ground. So which sum comes first?

ask.ifNot: The number of square metres is the area of the ground. For a rectangle, that is length times breadth.

beats.say: 30 times 20. 3 times 2 is 6, and the two zeros go on the end: 600 square metres.
Careful: 600 is the area, not the cost. Each of those 600 square metres costs 5 rupees.
6 times 5 is 30, so 600 times 5 is 3000. The levelling costs 3000 rupees.
Check by sharing the money back out. 3000 rupees divided by 5 rupees is 600 square metres, the area we found.
So it is always two steps: the area first, then area times the rate.
A square with an area of 144 square centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter needs the side. And the area of a square is side times side. So we want a number that, multiplied by itself, makes 144.
Let's get close first. 10 times 10 is 100. So what can we say about the side?

ask.ifNot: 100 is smaller than 144. So the side has to be a bit bigger than 10.

beats.say: 144 ends in 4, and 2 times 2 is 4. So let's try 12. 12 times 12 is 144, so the side is 12 centimetres.
Now the perimeter. A square has 4 equal sides, so which sum do we want?

ask.ifNot: The perimeter is the walk round all 4 sides. Each side is 12, so it is 4 times 12.

beats.say: 4 times 12 is 48. The perimeter is 48 centimetres.
Careful not to divide 144 by 4, and don't stop at 12. The side comes first, then all 4 sides. And the answer is a length, in centimetres.
Check by going backwards. 48 divided by 4 is 12, and 12 times 12 is 144, the area we were given.
Two steps to keep: the area tells you the side, and 4 times the side is the perimeter.
A triangle with an area of 5 square centimetres and a height of 2 centimetres. We want its base. It is isosceles, but that does not change the area rule.

board.text: Triangle: area 5 sq cm, height 2 cm. Base = ?

beats.say: The area of a triangle is half of base times height.
Put in what we know. 5 equals half, times the base, times 2.
Look at the half and the 2 on that line. What is half of 2?

ask.ifNot: Half of 2 means 2 split into two equal parts. Each part is 1.

beats.say: So the half and the 2 together make just 1. And 1 times the base is simply the base.
That leaves 5 equals the base. The base is 5 centimetres.
Check it in the rule. Half of 5 times 2 is half of 10, which is 5. That is our area.
The trap is to forget the half and say 5 divided by 2. The steady way is: double the area, then divide by the height.
So for a missing base, double the area and divide by the height.
A room has a floor 5 metres long and 4 metres wide. Its four walls have a total area of 108 square metres. How high is the room?

board.text: Floor 5 m × 4 m. Four walls: 108 sq m. Height = ?

beats.say: Imagine unfolding the four walls and laying them flat in a row. They make one long rectangle, exactly as tall as the room.
How long is that strip of walls?

ask.ifNot: The walls stand on the edges of the floor, all the way round. So the strip is as long as the walk round the floor, its perimeter.

beats.say: The floor's perimeter is 2 lengths and 2 breadths. 5 plus 4 is 9, and twice 9 is 18 metres.
So the strip is 18 metres long, and its area is 108. Length times height gives area.
The height is 108 divided by 18. Now 18 times 6 is 108, so the room is 6 metres high.
Check wall by wall. Two walls are 5 by 6, which is 30 each. Two are 4 by 6, which is 24 each. And 30, 30, 24 and 24 make 108.
The trap is dividing 108 by the floor area, 20. The walls stand on the floor's edges, so it is the perimeter we need.
So the area of four walls is the perimeter of the floor times the height. Divide to get the height back.
One side of a square grows by 50 percent, and the other shrinks by 50 percent. It becomes a rectangle. Is its area bigger, smaller, or the same?

board.text: Square: one side + 50%, the other side − 50%
New area: bigger, smaller or the same?

beats.say: No numbers are given, so let's choose an easy square. Say each side is 10. Its area is 10 times 10, which is 100.
50 percent means half. So what is 50 percent of 10?

ask.ifNot: 50 percent is the same as half. And half of 10 is 5.

beats.say: One side grows by 5: 10 plus 5 is 15. The other shrinks by 5: 10 minus 5 is 5.
One side went up by 5 and the other came down by 5. What do you think happens to the area?

ask.ifNot: It feels as if up 5 and down 5 should cancel out. But area multiplies the sides, so let's work it out and see.

beats.say: The new rectangle is 15 times 5, which is 75. And 75 is less than 100.
So the rectangle's area is smaller than the square's.

board.text: The new area is smaller than the square

beats.say: That is the trap: the same percent up and down does not cancel. One side became one and a half times as long, but the other became only half. Together that makes just three quarters of the square.
So when a question gives no numbers, pick easy ones and try it. The sums will show you what really happens.
A hall is 5 metres long and 4 metres wide. It is covered with square tiles of side 25 centimetres. How many tiles are needed?

board.text: Hall 5 m × 4 m, square tiles of side 25 cm. Tiles = ?

beats.say: Metres and centimetres are mixed, so first we make them match. 1 metre is 100 centimetres, so the hall is 500 centimetres by 400 centimetres.
How many 25 centimetre tiles fit in one row along the 500 centimetre length?

ask.ifNot: Four 25s make 100. There are 5 hundreds in 500, so that is 4 times 5, which is 20 tiles.

beats.say: 500 divided by 25 is 20 tiles in a row. And across the breadth, 400 divided by 25 is 16 rows.
So the floor is a grid of tiles: 16 rows, with 20 tiles in each row. 20 times 16 is 320 tiles.
Check it with areas. The floor is 500 times 400, which is 200000 square centimetres. One tile is 25 times 25, which is 625.
And 200000 divided by 625 is 320. The same answer both ways.
The trap is using 5 and 4 with 25 without changing units. Metres and centimetres must never be mixed in one sum.
So for tiles: same units first, count how many fit along each side, then multiply.
A wire 100 centimetres long is bent into a square. Then the same wire makes a rectangle, 5 centimetres longer and 5 centimetres narrower than the square.

board.text: Wire 100 cm, bent into a square
Rectangle: length = side + 5 cm, breadth = side − 5 cm

beats.say: The wire goes all the way round the square, so 100 centimetres is its perimeter. One side is 100 divided by 4, which is 25.
The area of the square is 25 times 25, which is 625 square centimetres.
Now the rectangle. Its length is 5 more than 25, and its breadth is 5 less than 25. What are they?

ask.ifNot: Both sides change. 25 plus 5 is 30 for the length, and 25 minus 5 is 20 for the breadth.

beats.say: So the rectangle is 30 by 20, and 30 times 20 is 600 square centimetres.
The difference is 625 minus 600, which is 25 square centimetres.
Don't answer 625 or 600. Those are the two areas, and the question wants the gap between them.
Notice something. Both shapes use the same wire: twice 30 plus 20 is 100 too. Yet the square holds more, by exactly 5 times 5.
So: the perimeter gives the side, the side gives each area, and then we subtract.
A triangle with a base of 5.2 centimetres and a height of 2.9 centimetres. We want its area.

board.text: Triangle: base 5.2 cm, height 2.9 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: The area of a triangle is half of base times height.
A smart move is to halve one of the numbers first. Which one halves more easily?

ask.ifNot: 5.2 ends in an even digit, so it halves neatly. 2.9 ends in an odd digit, so its half would be messier.

beats.say: Half of 5.2 is 2.6. So the area is 2.6 times 2.9.
Leave the decimal points out for a moment: 26 times 29. Now 26 times 30 is 780, and taking away one 26 leaves 754.
Time to put the point back. 2.6 and 2.9 have one decimal place each. So how many decimal places does the answer have?

ask.ifNot: Count the decimal places in both numbers: one, and one more. Together that makes 2 decimal places in the answer.

beats.say: So 754 becomes 7.54. The area is 7.54 square centimetres.
Does that look right? Half of 5 times 3 is 7 and a half, so 7.54 is sensible. And area is in square centimetres, not plain centimetres.
So for a triangle: halve the easy number, multiply, then count the decimal places.
A square with each side 6.1 centimetres. We want its area.
Which sum gives the area of a square?

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side is the walk round the edge, which is the perimeter. Area is the space inside: side times side.

beats.say: That is the trap in this question. 4 times 6.1 is 24.4, but that is the perimeter, a length.
So we need 6.1 times 6.1. Leave the points out for now: 61 times 61. Well, 61 times 60 is 3660, and one more 61 makes 3721.
Each 6.1 has one decimal place. So where does the point go in 3721?

ask.ifNot: One decimal place and one more make two. So count two digits from the right, and put the point there.

beats.say: That gives 37.21. The area is 37.21 square centimetres.
A quick sense check: 6 times 6 is 36, and 6.1 is a little more than 6. So a little more than 36 is just right.
So for the area of a square, multiply the side by itself, then count the decimal places in the answer.
A rectangle with a length of 1.1 centimetres and a breadth of 30 centimetres. We want its area.

board.text: Rectangle: length 1.1 cm, breadth 30 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Both sides are already in centimetres, so we can multiply straight away. Area is length times breadth.
1.1 is 1 whole and 1 tenth. What is 1 tenth of 30?

ask.ifNot: A tenth means divide by 10. And 30 divided by 10 is 3.

beats.say: So split the sum in two. 1 times 30 is 30, and 0.1 times 30 is 3.
30 plus 3 is 33. The area is 33 square centimetres.
Here is another way to see it. 11 times 30 is 330, and one decimal place brings that back to 33.
Watch the decimal point: it is 33, not 330. And we multiplied centimetres by centimetres, so the answer is in square centimetres.
So for an area with a decimal, split the decimal into its whole and its tenths, multiply each, and add.
A triangle with an area of 120 square centimetres and a base of 40 centimetres. We want its height.

board.text: Triangle: area 120 sq cm, base 40 cm. Height = ?

beats.say: The area of a triangle is half of base times height.
Put in what we know. Half of the base is half of 40, which is 20. So 20 times the height is 120.
20 times the height is 120. So how do we find the height?

ask.ifNot: 20 times something gives 120. To undo the times, we divide 120 by 20.

beats.say: 120 divided by 20 is 6. The height is 6 centimetres.
Now look at the choices: none of them says 6 centimetres. A height is a length, so which unit could be right?

ask.ifNot: Square units are for area. A height is a length, so it needs a plain length unit, like millimetres.

beats.say: 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres. So 6 centimetres is 6 times 10, which is 60 millimetres.
Check it in the rule. Half of 40 is 20, and 20 times 6 is 120. And mind the trap: 120 divided by 40 gives 3, which forgets the half.
So for a missing height: halve the base, divide the area by that, and then check which unit the answer is wanted in.
A square with a perimeter of 52 millimetres. We want its area.
Area needs the side, and all we have is the perimeter. So this takes two steps: first the side, then the area.
A square has 4 equal sides. How do we get one side from the perimeter?

ask.ifNot: The 4 equal sides add up to the perimeter. So one side is the perimeter shared among 4.

beats.say: 52 divided by 4 is 13. Each side is 13 millimetres.
Now for the area of the square. Which sum is it?

ask.ifNot: Area counts the little squares inside: 13 rows, with 13 in each row. That is side times side. 4 times the side only takes us back to the perimeter.

beats.say: 13 times 13. Take it in two bites: 13 times 10 is 130, and 13 times 3 is 39.
130 plus 39 is 169. The area is 169 square millimetres.
Look at the units. The side is in millimetres, so the area is in square millimetres. Not square centimetres, and not plain millimetres.
Check the first step: 4 sides of 13 make 52, the perimeter we were given.
So from perimeter to area in a square: divide by 4 for the side, then multiply the side by itself.
Meera starts with 30 packets. She gives away 2 groups of 6, and gets 3 groups of 4. Here is the whole story as one sum.
There is a minus, a plus and two times signs. What do we do first?

ask.ifNot: BODMAS puts multiplication before adding and subtracting. So the two times sums go first, wherever they sit in the line.

beats.say: 2 times 6 is 12. Those are the packets she gives away.
3 times 4 is also 12. Those are the packets she gets from her teacher.
Now the line is much simpler: 30 minus 12 plus 12.
Only a minus and a plus are left. Which way do we go?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so neither one jumps the queue. We simply work from left to right.

beats.say: 30 minus 12 is 18. Then 18 plus 12 is 30. Meera has 30 packets.
The trap is starting from the left with 30 minus 2, before the times sums are done. That mixes up loose packets with groups of packets.
It makes sense in the story too. She gave away 12 and got 12 back, so she still has her 30.
So: multiplications first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Riya buys 3 boxes of 12 diyas, gets 8 more, shares them into 4 rows, and adds 5 to each row. This sum tells the whole story.
Where do we start?

ask.ifNot: The B in BODMAS comes first, and B is for brackets. We finish everything inside them before we touch the rest.

beats.say: Inside the brackets there is a times and a plus. The times goes first: 3 times 12 is 36.
Then add the 8. 36 plus 8 is 44, and that is all of Riya's diyas.
The brackets are done, so the sum is now 44 divided by 4, plus 5. What comes next?

ask.ifNot: Division comes before addition. So we share the 44 into 4 rows first, and add the 5 afterwards.

beats.say: 44 divided by 4 is 11. That is 11 diyas in each row.
Then 5 more go into each row. 11 plus 5 is 16.
Here is the trap. Add the 4 and the 5 first, and you would be sharing 44 diyas among 9 rows. The story has only 4 rows.
So: brackets first, then divide and multiply, then add and subtract.
Priya's sum has every kind of sign in it, and brackets too. The order we work in decides the answer.
Brackets first, always. 2 plus 3 is 5.
Now there is a divide and a times, side by side. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Divide and multiply are equal partners, so we take them from left to right. The divide is on the left, so it goes first.

beats.say: 60 divided by 5 is 12. Then 12 times 4 is 48.
Careful here. If you multiplied the 5 by the 4 first, the 60 would be divided by a much bigger number, and the whole answer would change.
What is left is 48 minus 8 plus 5.
A minus and a plus now. Which one first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners too. So it is left to right again, and the minus is on the left.

beats.say: 48 minus 8 is 40, and 40 plus 5 is 45. Priya needs 45 packets.
So: brackets first. Then divide and multiply, left to right. Then add and subtract, left to right.
Here is the coach's formula for Rohit's score. It has brackets, a divide, a times and a minus.
What is the very first job?

ask.ifNot: The brackets are like a fence round 4 plus 2. Whatever is inside the fence gets done before anything else.

beats.say: 4 plus 2 is 6. So now we have 48 divided by 6, times 3, minus 5.
That was the trap. The 4 sits right next to the divide sign, so it is tempting to do 48 divided by 4. But the bracket has to be finished first.
Next there is a divide, a times and a minus. Which one now?

ask.ifNot: The minus waits till last. Divide and times are equal partners, so we take whichever comes first from the left, and that is the divide.

beats.say: 48 divided by 6 is 8. Then 8 times 3 is 24.
Last of all, the minus. 24 minus 5 is 19, so Rohit's score is 19.
So: brackets, then divide and multiply from left to right, and the minus right at the end.
Riya pays with a 100 rupee note. She buys 5 packets of samosas at 12 rupees each, then spends 8 rupees on chai. Here is the sum.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplication goes before subtraction. It fits the story too: we must know what the samosas cost before we take it off the 100.

beats.say: 5 times 12 is 60. That is the cost of the samosas.
Now there are two subtractions, and we go from left to right. 100 minus 60 is 40.
Then the chai. 40 minus 8 is 32, so Riya has 32 rupees left.
The classic slip is doing 100 minus 5 first, and then multiplying. That would leave Riya with far more money than the note she started with!
Check with the story. 60 for samosas and 8 for chai is 68 rupees spent. And 68 plus 32 makes the 100 rupee note.
So: do the times first, then the subtractions from left to right.
Ananya has 48 laddoos. She packs them equally into 6 boxes, and then her mom adds 5 more to each box. How many are in each box now?

board.text: 48 laddoos, 6 equal boxes, then 5 more in each box

beats.say: What happens first in the story?

ask.ifNot: Read it again: she packs the 48 into boxes first. Mom's extra laddoos come afterwards, when the boxes are already filled.

beats.say: So the sum is 48 divided by 6, plus 5.
BODMAS agrees with the story: divide before you add. 48 divided by 6 is 8, so there are 8 laddoos in each box.
Then mom adds 5 to each box. 8 plus 5 is 13 laddoos.
Here is the trap. The 5 goes into each box, so it is added after the sharing. Add 5 to the 48 first and you get 53, which is a different story.
Let's check by counting every laddoo. Mom gave 5 to each of the 6 boxes, which is 30. So there are 48 plus 30, 78 laddoos, and 6 boxes of 13 is 78 too.
So follow the story in order. And if you are unsure, BODMAS says the same thing: divide before you add.
